title: Locusts: Swarms Across Deserts
summary: How desert locusts change from shy loners into huge hungry swarms after rain, how they grow, how far they fly, and how countries work together to stop them.
poll: A tiny insect can be a bigger danger to farms than a large animal.

versions.title: Locusts on the Move
versions.text:
A locust is a kind of grasshopper. It lives in hot, dry lands. It has strong back legs. It has wings too.

Most of the time, it lives alone. It is green or brown. It stays away from the rest.

Then rain falls in the desert. Plants grow fast. Lots of eggs hatch. Then the plants dry up. The bugs must crowd close. Their legs bump. The bumps make them change! They turn yellow and black. Now they want to be in a big group.

A young locust has no wings. It is called a hopper. Hoppers march in big bands. They shed their skin five times. Then they have wings.

A huge group that flies is a swarm. A swarm can have more than a billion bugs. The wind helps it go far. It can fly a long way in a day.

Each one eats a lot. A swarm can eat a whole field of crops fast. Farms can lose all their food.

In 2018, big storms hit Saudi Arabia. Rain fell on the desert. Locusts grew there. Then swarms flew to lots of lands.

Now teams watch the desert. They look for young ones. They try to stop them fast.

versions.title: Locusts: Swarms Across Deserts
versions.text:
The desert locust is a kind of grasshopper that lives in hot, dry lands in parts of Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia. It has strong back legs for jumping and wings for flying. Most of the time, it is a harmless insect. But under the right conditions, it can become one of the most dangerous pests on Earth.

Usually, a desert locust is solitary, which means it lives alone. It is green or brown, and it avoids other locusts.

Everything changes after heavy rain falls in the desert. Plants grow quickly, and many locusts hatch. When the plants begin to dry up, the locusts crowd together on the last green patches. Their back legs keep bumping into each other, and this touching causes their bodies to change. They turn yellow and black, and they begin to seek out other locusts.

A young locust has no wings and is called a hopper. Hoppers march across the ground in large bands. As they grow, they molt, or shed their skin, five times. After the final molt, they have wings.

A huge group of flying locusts is called a swarm. One swarm can contain more than a billion insects. Carried by the wind, it can travel up to 150 kilometers in a single day.

Each locust eats about its own weight in plants every day. As a result, a swarm can strip a field of crops in hours, and farmers can lose their entire harvest.

In 2018, two cyclones brought heavy rain to the Empty Quarter, the great desert in the south of Saudi Arabia. Because the area was so remote, locusts bred there for months. Then swarms spread to many countries.

Today, teams watch the desert for signs of locusts. When they find hoppers, they spray a pesticide, a chemical that kills pests, to stop the swarms early.

versions.title: Locusts: Swarms Across Deserts
versions.text:
The desert locust is a type of grasshopper that inhabits hot, dry regions stretching across Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia. It has powerful back legs for jumping and wings for flying, and although it is usually a harmless insect, under certain conditions it can become one of the most destructive pests on Earth.

Usually, a desert locust is solitary, which means it lives alone, and because it is green or brown, it blends in with the desert while it avoids contact with other locusts.

Everything changes after heavy rain falls in the desert, because plants grow rapidly and many locusts hatch at the same time. When the vegetation begins to dry out, the locusts crowd together on the remaining green patches, where their back legs keep bumping into each other. This repeated touching triggers changes in their bodies and behavior, so they become gregarious, which means they prefer to live in groups. They turn yellow and black, and instead of avoiding other locusts, they begin to seek them out.

A young locust has no wings and is called a hopper. Hoppers march across the ground in large bands, eating as they travel, and as they grow, they molt, or shed their skin, five times before they finally have wings and can fly.

An enormous group of flying locusts is called a swarm. A single swarm can contain more than a billion insects, and when it is carried by the wind, it can travel up to 150 kilometers in one day.

Each locust consumes about its own weight in plants every day. Consequently, a swarm covering one square kilometer can eat as much food in a day as about 35,000 people, which means farmers can lose their entire harvest in a few hours.

In 2018, two cyclones brought heavy rain to the Empty Quarter, the vast desert in the south of Saudi Arabia. Because the area was too remote to monitor, locusts bred there for months, and when swarms later spread to many countries, Kenya faced its worst outbreak in about seventy years by 2020.

Today, teams monitor the desert and share reports through the United Nations, and when they discover hoppers, they spray a pesticide, a chemical that kills pests, so that the swarms are stopped before they form.

versions.title: Locusts: Swarms Across Deserts
versions.text:
The desert locust is a particular species of grasshopper that inhabits hot, arid regions stretching continuously across Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia, spanning an enormous geographic range that few other insects can match. It possesses powerful hind legs specifically adapted for jumping and wings well suited for sustained flight, and although it is ordinarily a comparatively harmless, unremarkable insect, under particular environmental conditions it can transform remarkably, almost overnight, into one of the most destructive agricultural pests found anywhere on the entire planet.

Ordinarily, a desert locust lives a solitary, independent existence, which means it functions entirely on its own without reference to others of its kind, and because its natural coloring is predominantly green or brown, it blends inconspicuously into the surrounding desert landscape while it deliberately and persistently avoids any direct contact with other locusts nearby.

Everything changes dramatically and rather suddenly after heavy rain eventually falls across the desert, because vegetation subsequently grows with remarkable rapidity and numerous locusts hatch simultaneously across a wide and often remote area. When the plants subsequently begin to dry out once again, the locusts congregate densely upon whatever green patches still remain, where their hind legs repeatedly and continuously bump against one another in close quarters. This constant, repeated physical contact triggers remarkable physiological and behavioral changes within their individual bodies, so they gradually become gregarious, meaning they come to actively prefer living in dense, crowded groups rather than alone. They characteristically turn yellow and black in coloration, and instead of continuing to avoid other locusts as before, they now actively and deliberately seek them out.

A young locust lacks wings entirely at this early stage and is accordingly termed a hopper. Hoppers march steadily and relentlessly across the ground in enormous, tightly coordinated bands, devouring vegetation voraciously as they travel onward across the landscape, and as they gradually develop and mature, they molt, or shed their outer exoskeleton, a total of five separate times before they eventually acquire fully functional wings capable of flight.

An immense group of flying locusts is formally designated a swarm, and a single such swarm can contain considerably more than a billion individual insects acting in concert, and when it is subsequently transported by prevailing winds across the region, it can travel up to 150 kilometers in a single day alone, covering vast distances with remarkable speed.

Each individual locust consumes approximately its own entire body weight in vegetation every single day without exception. Consequently, a swarm covering merely one square kilometer of ground can devour as much food in a single day as roughly 35,000 human beings would collectively consume, which means that agricultural communities can lose their entire annual harvest within merely a few catastrophic hours of a swarm's arrival.

In 2018, two separate cyclones delivered extraordinary, genuinely unprecedented rainfall to the Empty Quarter, the vast desert located in southern Saudi Arabia, and because this remote territory proved too inaccessible to monitor effectively at the time, locusts reproduced there completely undetected for several consecutive months, and when the resulting swarms subsequently spread across numerous countries, Kenya experienced its most serious locust outbreak in approximately seventy years by the year 2020, a crisis that affected millions of people's livelihoods.

Today, specialized monitoring teams carefully and continuously observe the desert and promptly share their observations through the United Nations, and whenever they discover hoppers congregating in significant numbers, they promptly apply a pesticide, a chemical substance specifically designed to kill pests, so that potential swarms are systematically eliminated well before they are ever able to fully form and spread.

Locusts can change after rain and form swarms that ruin crops.
Cyclones are the most dangerous storms on Earth.
Locusts can fly farther than any other kind of insect on Earth.
questions.why: The article explains how locusts change after rain, form swarms, damage harvests, and how teams try to stop them.

wrong.A: The article explains that locusts can become dangerous pests.
wrong.C: Cyclones are part of one example, not the main idea.
wrong.D: The article does not compare locusts with other insects.

questions.stem: How many times does a hopper molt before it has wings?
options: Two times
Ten times
Five times
One time
questions.why: The article says hoppers molt, or shed their skin, five times.

wrong.D: The article says hoppers molt more than once.

questions.stem: How far can a swarm travel in a single day?
options: Up to 150 kilometers
Up to 15 kilometers
Up to 1,500 kilometers
Only a few meters
questions.why: The article says a swarm carried by the wind can travel up to 150 kilometers in a day.

wrong.B: This is ten times less than the article states.
wrong.C: This is ten times more than the article states.
wrong.D: Swarms travel very far, not just a few meters.

questions.stem: The article says a desert locust is usually "solitary." Which phrase from the article helps explain this word?
options: it has powerful back legs
it turns yellow and black
it can fly up to 150 kilometers
it lives alone
questions.why: The article explains solitary right away with the phrase "which means it lives alone."

wrong.A: This describes its body, not how it lives.
wrong.B: This describes the change after crowding.
wrong.C: This describes swarms, not solitary locusts.

questions.stem: What causes a solitary locust to change into one that seeks out other locusts?
options: Eating too much pesticide in the fields
Repeated touching of its back legs in a crowd
Flying too far in one day
Living in a cold place
questions.why: When locusts crowd onto the last green patches, their back legs keep bumping, and this touching causes the change.

wrong.A: Pesticide kills locusts; it does not change them.
wrong.C: Flying far happens after the change, not before.
wrong.D: The article says locusts live in hot, dry places.

questions.stem: Why were the locusts in the Empty Quarter able to breed for months in 2018?
options: Farmers were feeding them grain every day.
The area was far away and hard to check.
The cyclones killed all the plants.
There was no rain at all that year.
questions.why: The article says the area was too remote to check or monitor, so no one stopped the breeding.

wrong.A: Nothing in the article says farmers fed locusts.
wrong.C: The rain made plants grow, which helped locusts.

questions.stem: Based on the article, which news report should worry locust teams the most?
options: Heavy rain has fallen in a remote desert.
A long, dry summer has begun in the desert.
A cold winter has arrived in the mountains.
A city has built a new airport.
questions.why: Heavy rain in the desert makes plants grow and many locusts hatch, which can lead to swarms.

wrong.B: Dry weather does not start a locust outbreak in the article.
wrong.C: The article does not link cold mountains with swarms.
wrong.D: An airport has nothing to do with locusts.

questions.stem: How is most of the article organized?
options: As a list of facts about many kinds of insects
As a story told by a farmer
As a series of steps that explain how locusts become swarms and spread
As an argument for and against pesticides
questions.why: The article moves in order: solitary locusts, rain, crowding, change, hoppers, swarms, damage, and control.

wrong.A: The article focuses on one insect, the desert locust.
wrong.D: Pesticides are mentioned at the end but not argued about.

MID.prompt: Explain why heavy rain in the desert can lead to problems for farmers far away. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained the chain of events from rain to swarms.
I used at least two details from the article.
I used words such as solitary, molt, or harvest correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: Heavy rain in the desert, sometimes brought by a cyclone, makes plants grow quickly and lets many locust eggs hatch at once. Each young locust, or hopper, molts five times as it grows, and because so many locusts are crowded together on the same shrinking patches of green plants, they stop being solitary and start forming massive bands. Once the locusts grow wings, the swarm can travel up to 150 kilometers in a single day, which means a problem that started in a remote desert can destroy another farmer's harvest far away before anyone even sprays a pesticide to stop it.

keyWords.definition: liking to live or be in groups
keyWords.example: Sheep are gregarious animals that stay close to the flock.

keyWords.definition: plants in general, especially those growing in an area
keyWords.example: After the spring rains, the valley was covered with green vegetation.

keyWords.definition: a sudden start or rise of something harmful, such as pests or a disease
keyWords.example: The school closed for a week because of a flu outbreak.

keyWords.definition: to watch or check something carefully over time
keyWords.example: Nurses monitor patients' heartbeats through the night.

keyWords.definition: to eat, drink, or use up
keyWords.example: Large cars consume more fuel than small ones.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the article?
options: Desert locusts are harmless insects that almost never leave the Empty Quarter in Saudi Arabia.
Kenya is the country most often harmed by locusts.
Crowding after rain makes locusts form swarms that destroy crops unless stopped early.
Cyclones form in the desert and carry locusts to Africa.
questions.why: The article traces how rain and crowding produce gregarious swarms, the damage they cause, and how teams monitor and spray hoppers.

wrong.A: The article explains how locusts spread to many countries.
wrong.B: Kenya is one example of an outbreak, not the main idea.
wrong.D: Cyclones brought rain; they did not carry locusts.

questions.stem: According to the article, a swarm covering one square kilometer can eat as much food in a day as about how many people?
questions.why: The article states that such a swarm eats as much in a day as about 35,000 people.

wrong.A: This number is ten times too small.
wrong.B: This number is ten times too large.
wrong.C: This number is far too small.

questions.stem: Which country faced its worst locust outbreak in about seventy years by 2020?
options: Kenya
Egypt
India
Morocco
questions.why: The article says that by 2020 Kenya experienced its worst outbreak in about seventy years.

wrong.B: Egypt is not named in the article.
wrong.C: India is not named in the article.
wrong.D: Morocco is not named in the article.

questions.stem: The article says crowded locusts become "gregarious." Which change best shows this?
options: They molt five times.
They seek out other locusts instead of avoiding them.
They turn green or brown and blend in with the sand.
They lose their wings.
questions.why: Gregarious means preferring to live in groups, which matches seeking out other locusts.

wrong.A: Molting is part of growing, not of being gregarious.
wrong.C: Green or brown is the color of solitary locusts.
wrong.D: Locusts gain wings; they do not lose them.

questions.stem: What chain of events led to swarms spreading to many countries after 2018?
options: Pesticides failed, so locusts left Saudi Arabia.
A long drought dried out the desert, so the locusts flew away to look for food elsewhere.
Farmers moved locusts to new fields.
Cyclone rain fed plants in a remote desert where locusts bred unseen.
questions.why: The article explains that cyclone rain fell on the Empty Quarter, the area was too remote to monitor, and locusts bred for months before spreading.

wrong.A: The article does not say pesticides failed.
wrong.B: The problem began with heavy rain, not drought.

questions.stem: Why does the article mention that locusts consume about their own weight in plants each day?
options: To show why even a single swarm can quickly destroy a harvest
To prove that locusts are heavier than other insects
To explain why locusts change color
To show that hoppers do not eat
questions.why: This fact, combined with the size of swarms, helps explain how farmers can lose a whole harvest in hours.

wrong.B: The article does not compare the weight of insects.
wrong.C: Color change is caused by crowding, not eating.
wrong.D: The article says hoppers eat as they travel.

questions.stem: Why is it wiser for teams to spray hoppers than flying swarms?
options: Hoppers are much larger and easier to see than adult locusts.
Pesticides only work on insects with wings.
Hoppers cannot fly yet, so they stay in one area.
Flying swarms do not eat crops.
questions.why: Hoppers cannot fly yet, so stopping them prevents swarms that could travel up to 150 kilometers a day.

wrong.A: The article does not say hoppers are larger.
wrong.B: Teams spray hoppers, which have no wings.
wrong.D: Flying swarms do consume huge amounts of crops.

questions.stem: Why does the article mention that teams share observations through the United Nations?
options: Locusts only live in one country.
Swarms cross borders, so countries need to warn one another.
The United Nations owns and controls all of the deserts.
Sharing reports makes it rain less.
questions.why: Because swarms can fly far and spread to many countries, sharing information helps countries prepare and act early.

wrong.A: Desert locusts live across Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia.
wrong.C: Nothing in the article says this.
wrong.D: Sharing reports cannot change the weather.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say the best way to fight locusts is to wait and spray the swarms when they reach farms. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that the best strategy is to wait and spray locust swarms once they reach farms, because by that point the damage is already nearly impossible to stop. The article explains that a single swarm can contain more than a billion insects, and because each locust can consume roughly its own weight in vegetation every day, a swarm can strip an entire field within hours of arriving. Once locusts turn gregarious and begin forming bands of hoppers, it is far more effective to monitor the desert for the earliest signs of an outbreak and spray the young hoppers before they even grow wings. The 2018 outbreak that began in Saudi Arabia's Empty Quarter shows exactly why early action matters, because the area was too remote to check, locusts bred undisturbed for months, and the swarms eventually spread across many countries.
